intro: The Talmud argues. It records questions, proofs, objections and answers, and it often keeps several views side by side. Yet Jewish communities have needed to know what to do on a given day. This unit asks how the rabbis reasoned from a verse to a rule, and how those rules traveled into codes and letters that people still consult.

You will study Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules and Rabbi Akiva's close reading, then map how a sugya moves. You will follow the path from the Geonim and Alfasi to Maimonides's Mishneh Torah and Karo's Shulchan Arukh. Then you will read responsa, look at custom, and see how Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Jews reason about electricity, medicine and women's leadership.

By the end, you will be able to trace a ruling from its source to a code, explain why authorities disagree, and describe each movement's view in its own terms. You will also ask, every time, what a ruling protects: the worker, the patient, the stranger, or the life at risk.
bigQuestion: How does Talmudic reasoning turn ancient texts into guidance for new cases, and why do careful readers reach different answers?

title: Talmudic Reasoning and Halakhah

chapters.title: The Thirteen Rules, Logic and the Codes
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the rabbis reason from a verse to a rule, and how does that rule travel from a Talmud page into daily practice?

story.title: Thirteen Rules Before Breakfast
story.kicker: Many Jews recite a list of reasoning rules every morning, and few stop to ask what the list is doing there.
paragraphs: In many synagogues, the morning service moves quickly. Near the start, the prayer book prints a short paragraph that looks out of place. It is not a praise or a request. It begins, in paraphrase, "Rabbi Ishmael says: the Torah is interpreted by thirteen rules." Then it lists them.

A high school student in a Chicago congregation follows along one weekday. She reads "from light to heavy" and "from the general to the particular." She wonders why a list of logic rules sits between blessings. Her grandfather tells her that the rabbis put study inside prayer, so that every day begins with a piece of learning.

The list comes from the Sifra, an early rabbinic commentary on Leviticus. Rabbinic tradition treats the rules as the tools a reader uses to draw laws out of the Torah's words. Some rules compare two cases. Some weigh a general statement against a specific one. Each rule is a way of arguing.

This chapter follows those tools from the verse to the Talmud page, and then from the page to the great law codes. By the end, you will be able to trace how a single rule, like returning a lost object, moved from a sugya into a book that people consult today.
story.think: Why might a community choose to recite rules of reasoning inside its daily prayers, and what does that choice show about how it values study?

lessons.title: Rabbi Ishmael's Thirteen Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules are a rabbinic list of methods for drawing laws from the Torah's words.
reading: The *thirteen rules* are attributed to Rabbi Ishmael, a *tanna* of the early second century CE. A tanna is a teacher of the Mishnah period. The list opens the Sifra, a rabbinic commentary on Leviticus. Many prayer books print it in the morning service, so it is read daily by many who pray.

The rules are called *middot*, a Hebrew word that here means measures or methods. They are not new laws. They are ways to reason from the text. One rule compares a lighter case to a heavier one. Another links two passages that use the same word. Others settle how a general statement relates to a list of details.

Rabbinic tradition holds that these methods help show what the Torah's words imply. Academic historians see them as a record of how early rabbis argued, with parallels in Greek and Roman legal reasoning. Readers across Orthodox, Conservative and Reform settings study the list, though they differ on how much authority the results carry.

words.d: the list of methods for interpreting the Torah that rabbinic tradition attributes to Rabbi Ishmael
a rabbinic teacher of the Mishnah period, roughly the first two centuries CE
measures or methods; here, the rules the rabbis used to reason from a verse

check.why: The middot are ways to interpret, not laws in themselves.

lessons.title: From Light to Heavy
lessons.mainIdea: Kal va-chomer argues that if a rule holds in a lighter case, it holds all the more in a weightier one.
reading: The first of the thirteen rules is *kal va-chomer*, which means "light and heavy." English speakers call it an argument a fortiori. If something is true in the easier case, it must be true in the harder case too. The rabbis found this pattern already inside the Hebrew Bible.

A well-known example is Numbers 12:14. Miriam has spoken against Moses and is struck with a skin disease. God says, in paraphrase, that if her father had spit in her face, she would hide in shame for seven days. How much more, then, should she stay apart after God's rebuke. Rabbinic lists count this verse among the Torah's own kal va-chomer arguments.

The rabbis also limited the rule. A principle called *dayo* says a conclusion drawn this way cannot be stronger than the case it came from. So Miriam stays apart seven days, not fourteen. The Gemara discusses this limit in Bava Kamma 25a, where it uses the Miriam verse. The limit keeps an argument from growing past its evidence.

words.d: light and heavy; an argument that what holds in a lesser case holds all the more in a greater one
Latin for "from the stronger"; the English name for a light-to-heavy argument
"it is enough"; the rule that a light-to-heavy conclusion cannot go beyond its source case

look.prompt: Explain the light case and the heavy case in this verse. Then explain why dayo keeps the answer at seven days.

check.why: Kal va-chomer means light and heavy, the a fortiori argument.

check.q: Which verse do rabbinic lists count as a kal va-chomer inside the Torah?

choices: It keeps the conclusion from being stronger than the source case

check.why: Dayo, discussed in Bava Kamma 25a, says the conclusion is enough at the level of its source.

lessons.title: Analogy and General Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Gezerah shavah links two passages by a shared word, and the general-and-particular rules decide how a broad statement relates to a list.
reading: The second rule is *gezerah shavah*, often translated "equal decree" or verbal analogy. When the same word appears in two passages, a law known in one may be applied to the other. The Talmud treats this rule with care. In Pesachim 66a, a teacher may use a gezerah shavah only if he received it from his teachers, not one he invented.

Several rules deal with *klal u-frat*, the general and the particular. Suppose a verse names a broad category and then lists examples. Rabbi Ishmael's school often reads the list as limiting the category to those examples. When the verse adds another broad phrase after the list, the category widens to things like the examples.

These rules can sound technical, but they answer a real problem. Every legal text must be applied to cases it never names. The rabbis built tools so that new cases could be judged by the text, not by one judge's mood. Readers who disagree still share the tools, which lets them argue about the same words.

words.d: verbal analogy; applying a law from one passage to another that uses the same word
the general and the particular; rules for how a broad term relates to a list of examples
teaching received from earlier teachers; the Talmud limits some methods to what was received

lessons.title: Rabbi Akiva and Every Letter
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbinic tradition remembers Rabbi Akiva as reading meaning into even the smallest features of the Torah's text.
reading: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ishmael were contemporaries in the early second century. The Talmud remembers them as holding different styles. A saying attributed to Rabbi Ishmael holds that "the Torah speaks in human language," so repeated words may simply be normal speech. Rabbi Akiva's school often drew a lesson from each extra word or letter.

Menachot 29b tells an *aggadah*, a rabbinic story, about this. Moses finds God tying small crowns on the letters of the Torah. God explains that one day a man named Akiva will derive heaps of laws from each crown. Moses is brought to sit in the back of Akiva's class. He cannot follow the discussion and feels faint. Then a student asks Akiva for his source, and Akiva answers that it is a law given to Moses at Sinai.

Readers take the story in different ways. Many traditional readers see it as a claim that later study unfolds what was given at Sinai. Some modern readers see it as the rabbis admitting that their methods had changed the text's meaning over time. The story holds both readings open, which may be why it is taught so often.

words.d: the non-legal parts of rabbinic literature: stories, sayings and teachings about ethics and belief
a leading tanna of the early second century CE, remembered for reading meaning into every detail of the text
a tanna of the early second century CE to whom tradition attributes the thirteen rules

lessons.title: Mapping the Moves
lessons.mainIdea: A sugya moves by question, proof, objection and answer, and sometimes ends with the question still open.
reading: A *sugya* is one unit of Talmudic discussion on a single topic. It usually starts from a Mishnah or a *baraita*, a teaching of the tannaim left out of the Mishnah. The Gemara then asks a question. Someone offers a proof. Another voice raises an objection, called a *kushya*. An answer follows, and the cycle may repeat many times.

Some sugyot end in a ruling. Others end with the word *teiku*, meaning "let it stand." The question is left open. Later scholars built a popular folk reading of teiku as an acronym that says the prophet Elijah will answer it. The plain sense is simpler: the Talmud records that the rabbis did not settle it.

Mapping a sugya means labeling each step: who speaks, what they claim, and what source they bring. Students in a *chavruta*, a study pair, often draw arrows between steps. The map shows that rejected answers stay on the page. The Talmud keeps the minority view and the failed proof, because the argument itself is part of what it teaches.

words.d: one unit of Talmudic discussion on a single topic
a difficulty or objection raised against a claim in the Gemara
"let it stand"; the Talmud's way of leaving a question unresolved
a study partner or pair who read a text aloud and argue it together

look.title: Label the Steps
look.text: Step A: the Mishnah states a rule. Step B: the Gemara asks where the rule comes from. Step C: a rabbi cites a verse. Step D: another rabbi says the verse is needed for a different law. Step E: the Gemara finds a second verse. Step F: a new question is asked and left as teiku.
look.prompt: Label each step as rule, question, proof, objection, answer or open question. Which step is the kushya?

check.why: A baraita is an outside tannaitic teaching the Gemara often quotes.

check.q: Why do rejected answers stay on the Talmud page?
choices: They were added by later censors

check.why: The Talmud records failed proofs and minority views as part of its method.

lessons.title: Who Is Speaking, and When
lessons.mainIdea: Knowing whether a voice is a tanna, an amora or the anonymous Gemara helps a reader weigh each step.
reading: The Talmud's voices come from different layers. The tannaim taught up to about 200 CE, when the Mishnah was edited. The *amoraim*, teachers in the Land of Israel and in Babylonia, taught from about 200 to 500 CE. Rav and Shmuel, Abaye and Rava are famous Babylonian amoraim.

Many lines have no name at all. Scholars call this the anonymous voice, or *stam*. It asks questions and links statements together. Some academic scholars, such as David Weiss Halivni, argued that much of this voice was added by later editors after the named amoraim. Other scholars date it differently.

The layers matter for reasoning. An amora usually cannot overrule a tanna. So if an amora's view seems to contradict a Mishnah, the Gemara will work hard to reconcile them. Knowing who is speaking shows why the Gemara worries about some contradictions and not others.

words.d: a rabbinic teacher of the Gemara period, roughly 200 to 500 CE, in the Land of Israel or Babylonia
the anonymous voice of the Gemara that asks questions and connects statements
the discussion of the Mishnah by the amoraim and later editors; with the Mishnah it forms the Talmud

lessons.title: The Brisker Method in Brief
lessons.mainIdea: The Brisker method analyzes a law by splitting it into precise concepts to explain why authorities disagree.
reading: In the late nineteenth century, Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik taught in Brisk, a town now called Brest in Belarus. His method of study became known as the *Brisker method*. It asks what exact concept lies under a law. It often divides one rule into two parts, each with its own logic.

A common Brisker move is the *two dinim*, or two laws. Is an obligation about the person, or about the object? Is a ritual about the act, or about the result? When two authorities seem to disagree, a Brisker reader asks whether they are really answering different conceptual questions. Maimonides's code is a favorite subject for this kind of analysis.

Supporters say the method makes reasoning exact, like analytic philosophy. Critics say it can impose modern categories on ancient texts. Academic scholars often read the same sugya historically instead, asking how it grew. Both kinds of reader are asking why the text says what it says, by different roads.

words.d: a style of Talmud analysis from Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik of Brisk that defines the precise concepts under a law
"two laws"; the Brisker move of splitting one rule into two distinct legal ideas
Jewish law as developed in the Talmud and later rabbinic works

look.title: Person or Object?

check.q: What is one criticism of the Brisker method?
choices: It may impose modern categories on ancient texts

check.why: Critics argue its conceptual categories can be foreign to the texts' own time.

sections.title: From the Page to the Code

lessons.title: The Geonim and the Rif
lessons.mainIdea: The Geonim and then Alfasi began turning Talmudic discussion into rulings people could follow.
reading: After the Talmud was completed, the heads of the Babylonian academies were called *Geonim*, from about 600 to 1040 CE. Jews in distant lands sent them questions, and they answered with rulings drawn from the Talmud. Their letters are among the earliest responsa.

Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, known as the *Rif* (1013–1103), lived in North Africa and later Spain. He wrote a shortened Talmud. He kept the legal discussion needed to reach a ruling and left out most of the aggadah and the side debates. His work is printed in the back of many Talmud volumes.

The Rif shows a basic problem. The Talmud argues but does not always decide. Someone must read the whole debate and say which view is followed. Every later code faced this task, and every code made choices that other scholars questioned. That is why codes often arrived with critics beside them.

words.d: heads of the Babylonian academies after the Talmud, about 600 to 1040 CE
Rabbi Isaac Alfasi (1013–1103), who wrote a shortened legal digest of the Talmud
a decision about which view in a debate is followed in practice

look.title: What Would You Cut?

look.prompt: What would you keep and what would you cut? What might be lost, as the Rif's critics noted?

lessons.title: Maimonides's Mishneh Torah
lessons.mainIdea: Maimonides's Mishneh Torah, completed c. 1180, organized all of Jewish law by topic without the arguments.
reading: Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, called Maimonides or the Rambam, lived from 1138 to 1204, in Spain, Morocco and Egypt. Around 1180 he completed the *Mishneh Torah*, a code in fourteen books. It covers all of Jewish law, including laws for the Temple that were not practiced in his day.

The code is organized by subject, written in clear Mishnaic Hebrew, and gives rulings without citing the debate. In his introduction, Maimonides says a reader could learn the written Torah and then this book, and know the whole Oral Law. That claim upset many scholars.

Critics such as Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières, the *Rabad*, wrote sharp glosses against him. They worried that a code without sources would cut readers off from the Talmud and hide the reasons for a ruling. Today the Rabad's glosses are printed beside the Mishneh Torah, so the argument sits on the same page.

words.d: Maimonides's fourteen-book code of Jewish law, completed c. 1180
Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, Maimonides (1138–1204)
Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières, a critic whose glosses are printed beside the Mishneh Torah

look.prompt: Why might this claim worry scholars who valued Talmud study? What might it offer a reader far from a teacher?

lessons.title: The Tur and the Shulchan Arukh
lessons.mainIdea: The Tur's four parts shaped the Shulchan Arukh of 1565, and Isserles's gloss added Ashkenazi practice.
reading: Rabbi Jacob ben Asher wrote the *Arba'ah Turim*, or Tur, in the fourteenth century. He limited it to laws in practice and divided it into four parts. Orach Chayim covers daily life and holidays. Yoreh De'ah covers topics like food and mourning. Even ha-Ezer covers marriage. Choshen Mishpat covers civil law and courts.

Rabbi Joseph Karo (1488–1575), living in Safed, wrote a long commentary on the Tur. He then made a brief summary called the *Shulchan Arukh*, "the set table," first printed in 1565. Karo's rulings usually follow the majority of three earlier authorities: the Rif, Maimonides and the Rosh.

Rabbi Moses Isserles of Kraków, called the Rema, added a gloss called the Mappah, "tablecloth." It records where Ashkenazi practice differs. Printed together, the two became the standard code for many communities. Later commentaries surround them on the page, and the debate continues around the set table.

words.d: Arba'ah Turim, the fourteenth-century code by Jacob ben Asher in four parts
"the set table"; Joseph Karo's code, first printed in 1565
"tablecloth"; Moses Isserles's gloss on the Shulchan Arukh recording Ashkenazi practice

chapters.title: Responsa, Custom and Modern Questions
chapters.bigQuestion: How do rabbis reason from ancient sources to questions the Talmud never imagined, and why do different movements reach different answers?

story.title: Is a Light Switch a Fire?
story.kicker: A short question about a lamp can bring back a long answer built from Talmud, codes and science.
paragraphs: Imagine a letter arriving at a rabbi's home in the early twentieth century. Electric lights are new in the town. A family asks a short question. May they turn a lamp on or off on Shabbat, the day of rest?

The rabbi cannot look up the answer. The Talmud never mentions electricity. So he reads the Mishnah's list of the thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat, in Shabbat 7:2. He asks whether a glowing wire is like kindling a fire. He asks whether closing a circuit is like building, or like finishing an object.

He also reads what earlier authorities wrote about similar cases, such as heating metal. He learns how the lamp actually works. Page after page, he weighs one comparison against another. His answer is a *responsum*, a written reply to a question of Jewish law.

Rabbis answering this question did not all agree, and they still do not. This chapter looks at how responsa work, what custom adds, and how Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Jews reason from the same sources toward different answers about modern life.
story.think: What does a rabbi need to know besides the Talmud to answer a question about a new technology?

sections.title: A Question Sent, an Answer Reasoned

lessons.title: What a Responsum Is
lessons.mainIdea: A responsum is a written answer to a question of Jewish law, reasoned from the Talmud and later sources.
reading: The *responsa* literature began with the Geonim of Babylonia, who answered letters from Jewish communities across North Africa, Spain and beyond. A famous example is the letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, written in 987, answering how the Mishnah and Talmud were composed. Historians still use it.

In Hebrew the genre is called *she'elot u-teshuvot*, "questions and answers." A community or a person writes a question. A rabbi answers, citing the Talmud, the codes and earlier responsa. Many thousands of responsa survive, from the Middle Ages to today.

Responsa show halakhah meeting real life. They record trade disputes, family crises, plagues, migrations and inventions. For historians, they are a window on daily Jewish life. For many Jewish communities, they are how the law is applied to a case that the codes did not foresee.

words.d: a written answer by a rabbi to a question of Jewish law; the plural is responsa
"questions and answers"; the Hebrew name for the responsa literature
heads of the Babylonian academies, about 600 to 1040 CE, who wrote early responsa

lessons.title: How a Responsum Is Built
lessons.mainIdea: A responsum states the question, gathers the sources, weighs the comparisons and then rules, often with a note of caution.
reading: Most responsa follow a pattern. First the rabbi restates the question, sometimes asking about facts. Then he gathers sources: the relevant Mishnah and Gemara, the Rif, Maimonides, the Tur and Shulchan Arukh, and earlier responsa. He looks for the closest case, or *precedent*.

The heart of the answer is comparison. Is the new case like the old one or different? The rabbi uses the same moves as a sugya: question, proof, objection, answer. He may note a minority view and say when it can be relied on, such as in cases of great need or loss.

Many responsa end with a ruling and a word of warmth for the person asking. Some rabbis write that they are ruling for this case only. That caution reflects a Talmudic habit: a ruling depends on its facts, and a different case may need a new answer. Readers are asked to check whether their own case truly matches.

words.d: an earlier case or ruling used to decide a new one
an opinion not followed as the main ruling but kept in the sources and sometimes relied on in need
a rabbi who decides questions of Jewish law

look.title: Order the Steps
look.text: A posek receives a question. He (1) rules for this case only, (2) finds a Mishnah on a similar case, (3) asks the family one fact about the situation, (4) checks what Maimonides and the Shulchan Arukh say, (5) notes a minority view for great need.

choices: A rabbi who decides questions of Jewish law

choices: Comparing the new case to earlier cases

lessons.title: Respondents Across the Centuries
lessons.mainIdea: Great respondents in every age, from Babylonia to New York, applied the Talmud to the questions of their own time.
reading: Rabbi Solomon ibn Adret of Barcelona, the *Rashba* (c. 1235–1310), answered questions from across Europe and North Africa. Thousands of his responsa survive. His contemporary Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, the *Rosh*, moved from Germany to Toledo and answered questions there. His son wrote the Tur.

In the twentieth century, Rabbi Moshe Feinstein (1895–1986) of New York became one of the most consulted Orthodox authorities in America. His responsa, *Iggerot Moshe*, address questions about modern medicine, American work life and new technology. Rabbi Ovadia Yosef in Israel wrote widely for Sephardic Jews.

The Conservative movement's Committee on Jewish Law and Standards issues responsa voted on by a panel of rabbis. The Reform movement has also published responsa, which draw on the tradition as guidance rather than binding law. The genre is shared, even when the view of authority differs.

words.d: Rabbi Solomon ibn Adret of Barcelona (c. 1235–1310), author of thousands of responsa
the collected responsa of Rabbi Moshe Feinstein (1895–1986) of New York

words.w: Committee on Jewish Law and Standards
words.d: the Conservative movement's panel that issues responsa

lessons.title: Minhag: The Custom of the Place
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah gives local custom real weight, and one clear case protects workers.
reading: *Minhag* means custom. It is a practice a community keeps, often for generations, even where the Talmud does not require it. The Mishnah already gives custom weight. Mishnah Pesachim 4:1 says that where people are used to working on the morning before Passover, they may work, and where they are not, they may not.

Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:1 applies custom to work and wages. An employer who hires workers cannot force them to start earlier or stay later than the local custom. Where the custom is to feed workers, he must feed them. The Mishnah protects the worker's expectations from the employer's power.

Later authorities treat custom seriously, and some say an old custom of Israel has the force of law. Others warn that a custom with no basis, or one that causes harm, should not be followed. The tension between honoring practice and testing it by the sources runs through halakhah.

words.d: custom; a practice a community keeps, which halakhah often honors
"the middle gate"; a tractate on lost objects, loans, work and wages
the accepted practice of a particular place, which can set terms like work hours

look.title: The Workers' Custom

look.prompt: Whose side does this Mishnah protect, and how does custom do the protecting?

lessons.title: Different Customs, Same Law
lessons.mainIdea: Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities keep different customs while studying the same Talmud and codes.
reading: Jewish communities spread across many lands and grew different customs. *Ashkenazi* Jews trace their roots to Central and Eastern Europe. *Sephardi* Jews trace theirs to Spain and Portugal, and many settled in North Africa and the Ottoman lands. Mizrahi Jews come from communities across the Middle East.

A well-known example is *kitniyot*, legumes such as rice and beans, on Passover. Many Ashkenazi communities have the custom not to eat them. Many Sephardi communities do eat them. Both study the same Talmud. The difference comes from custom, and each community respects the other's.

This is why Isserles's gloss matters. Karo's Shulchan Arukh often follows Sephardic practice. Isserles notes where Ashkenazi custom differs. The printed page holds two communities side by side, and neither is ranked above the other. A reader can see at a glance how each community practices.

words.d: Jews whose families trace their roots to Central and Eastern Europe
Jews whose families trace their roots to Spain and Portugal
legumes such as rice and beans; many Ashkenazi Jews have the custom not to eat them on Passover

look.title: Two Seders
look.text: Two friends host Passover seders on the same street. At one table, rice is served. At the other, there is no rice, and the host explains it is her family's custom. Both hosts keep the same laws of matzah from the Talmud.
look.prompt: Explain the difference using the words law and custom. Why might the Talmud's respect for local custom help neighbors respect each other?

check.q: What causes the difference over kitniyot on Passover?

lessons.title: Electricity on Shabbat
lessons.mainIdea: Authorities reason about electricity by comparing it to the Mishnah's kinds of Shabbat work, and they reach different answers.
reading: Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists thirty-nine main kinds of work, the *melakhot*, forbidden on Shabbat. They include kindling a fire, building and finishing an object, the final hammer blow that completes a thing. Electricity is not on the list, so authorities ask which melakhah it most resembles.

Among Orthodox authorities, many hold that making a filament glow is like kindling. The Chazon Ish, Rabbi Avraham Yeshayahu Karelitz, compared closing a circuit to building. Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach of Jerusalem questioned that comparison and discussed other grounds. In practice, Orthodox communities generally do not operate electric devices on Shabbat.

In 1950 the Conservative movement's law committee accepted a responsum permitting electric lights on Shabbat, reasoning that electricity is not fire. Reform Judaism generally leaves such choices to the individual, guided by the goals of rest and holiness. Each movement reads the same Mishnah, then weighs it with its own view of authority.

words.d: one of the thirty-nine kinds of creative work the Mishnah lists as forbidden on Shabbat
the weekly day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday night
Rabbi Avraham Yeshayahu Karelitz (1878–1953), an Orthodox authority who compared closing a circuit to building

check.why: The Chazon Ish compared completing a circuit to building.

lessons.title: Saving a Life: Organ Donation
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud's rule that saving a life overrides almost every law shapes modern debates on organ donation and brain death.
reading: The Talmud treats *pikuach nefesh*, saving a life, as overriding nearly every other law. In Yoma 85b, rabbis offer several verses as proof. Shmuel cites Leviticus 18:5, "he shall live by them," and reads it to mean live by the laws, not die because of them. The Gemara prefers his proof.

Yoma 85a also discusses a person trapped under a collapsed building on Shabbat. How far must rescuers dig to check for life? One view says to the nose, since breathing shows life. Modern authorities have used this passage when asking what counts as death, and whether brain death meets the test.

In 1986 the Chief Rabbinate of Israel accepted brain-stem death under conditions, which allows heart donation. Some Orthodox authorities disagree and accept only the stopping of the heart. Conservative and Reform bodies have issued responsa supporting organ donation as saving life. Each position cites the same sugya.

words.d: saving a life; the principle that it overrides almost every other commandment
the complete and lasting loss of brain function; debated in halakhah as a definition of death
"the day"; the tractate on Yom Kippur, which includes the discussion of saving life

look.prompt: How does Shmuel turn "live by them" into a rule that saving a life overrides Shabbat?

check.why: Shmuel cites "he shall live by them," Leviticus 18:5.

check.why: Checking breath at the nose shapes debates about brain death.

lessons.title: Medicine and Technology
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbis weigh new medicine and technology by the value of each life and by Talmudic cases that seem closest.
reading: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches that whoever saves one life is regarded as if they saved a whole world. It explains that humanity began with one person. Many medical responsa quote it. It frames every patient as a whole world, which shapes questions of care at the end of life.

Modern responsa cover fertility treatment, genetic testing, vaccination and end-of-life care. A posek often asks a doctor to explain the facts first. Then the posek compares the case to a Talmudic one, such as healing on Shabbat or the duty to seek a physician.

Technology raises different questions: automatic timers on Shabbat, hearing aids, video calls for a minyan during a pandemic. Answers vary across movements and even within one movement. The pattern stays the same: learn the facts, find the closest source, and weigh what the ruling protects.

words.d: the high court; the tractate on courts, testimony and the value of each life
a quorum of ten adults for communal prayer
medical treatment and comfort for a person near death, a frequent subject of responsa

look.title: A Whole World
look.text: Humanity was created from a single person to teach that whoever destroys one life is regarded as having destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life is regarded as having saved a whole world.
look.prompt: Why might a doctor or a posek keep this Mishnah in mind when a single patient's care is costly or uncertain?

check.q: What does Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 compare one life to?
check.why: The Mishnah says saving one life is like saving a whole world.

check.q: What does a posek usually do first with a medical question?
choices: Learn the medical facts from a doctor
check.why: Rulings depend on facts, so the posek learns them first.

check.q: What is a minyan?
choices: A quorum of ten for communal prayer

lessons.title: Women's Torah Study and Ordination
lessons.mainIdea: Movements read the same sources on women's learning and leadership and reach different conclusions.
reading: Mishnah Sotah 3:4 records a disagreement. Ben Azzai says a person should teach his daughter Torah. Rabbi Eliezer opposes it. Later codes mostly followed Rabbi Eliezer's caution. Yet the Talmud also remembers Beruriah, a learned woman whose rulings and sharp answers it quotes.

In the twentieth century, women's Torah study grew across movements. Reform ordained Sally Priesand as a rabbi in 1972. Reconstructionist Judaism ordained Sandy Eisenberg Sasso in 1974. The Conservative Jewish Theological Seminary voted in 1983 to ordain women, and Amy Eilberg was ordained in 1985.

Within Orthodoxy, advanced Talmud study for women has grown in many schools. Clergy roles remain debated. Yeshivat Maharat, founded in 2009, trains Orthodox women as clergy. Many Orthodox authorities oppose that step. Each side reasons from the same sources, Sotah 3:4 among them.

words.d: a tractate that includes the Mishnah's debate between Ben Azzai and Rabbi Eliezer about teaching daughters Torah
a learned woman of the second century remembered in the Talmud for her knowledge and wit
semikhah; formal recognition that a person may serve as a rabbi

check.why: Ben Azzai supports teaching daughters Torah; Rabbi Eliezer opposes.

check.q: Which movement ordained the first woman rabbi in this lesson's list, in 1972?
check.why: Reform ordained Sally Priesand in 1972.

check.q: Who is Beruriah?
choices: The author of the Shulchan Arukh

lessons.title: How Movements Read Authority
lessons.mainIdea: Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Jews share the Talmud but differ on how binding its law is and who may change it.
reading: Orthodox Judaism generally holds halakhah binding and sees change as possible only within the rules of the tradition. A posek works from the Talmud and codes, and respects the rulings of earlier generations. Modern Orthodox and Haredi communities differ on many questions.

Conservative Judaism holds halakhah binding while viewing it as developing over history. Its law committee may accept more than one responsum on a question, and a local rabbi chooses among them. Reform Judaism views Jewish law as a guide, stressing personal choice informed by study and ethics.

These views shape how a sugya is read. An Orthodox reader asks what the law requires. A Conservative reader may also ask how the law grew historically. A Reform reader may ask what value the law protects today. All three may sit at the same table in a chavruta and read the same daf, a page of Talmud.

words.d: movements that generally hold halakhah binding and changeable only within the tradition's own rules
a movement that holds halakhah binding while viewing it as developing over history
a movement that treats Jewish law as a guide for personal choice informed by study and ethics
a two-sided leaf, or page, of the Talmud

lessons.title: Reading a Responsum in Paraphrase
lessons.mainIdea: Reading a responsum means following its question, sources, comparisons and ruling, and noticing what it protects.
reading: Here is a simple kind of case many responsa address. A patient is fasting on Yom Kippur. The doctor says fasting may endanger the patient. The patient asks whether to eat. The posek begins with Mishnah Yoma 8:5, which says a sick person is fed on the advice of experts.

The posek then turns to Yoma 83a, which says that if the patient says he needs food, he is fed even against a doctor's opinion. The reasoning is that "the heart knows its own bitterness," a verse from Proverbs 14:10. Later codes follow this rule, and the Shulchan Arukh records it in Orach Chayim 618.

The ruling protects the person in danger and trusts their own sense of need. A student reading such a responsum should mark each step: question, Mishnah, Gemara, code, ruling. Then ask what the ruling protects. In this case, argument and mercy point the same way.

words.d: the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and prayer
the part of the Tur and Shulchan Arukh on daily life, prayer, Shabbat and holidays
in the Mishnah, a person with knowledge of healing whose advice guides the ruling

look.title: The Heart Knows
